key_points.point: The report highlights that AI presents extraordinary opportunities for individualized tutoring, coaching, and a dramatic acceleration of research across disciplines. The committee argues that seizing these opportunities demands bold thinking so that students are prepared with a sophisticated understanding of AI's potential. Rather than rejecting the technology, the institution seeks to employ AI to augment human capabilities and drive forward fields of inquiry. However, this acceleration must be balanced with foundational human development and the core mission of residential education.
key_points.verbatim: AI also presents extraordinary opportunities, from unprecedented possibilities for individualized tutoring and coaching to a dramatic acceleration and revamping of research in many disciplines. Seizing these opportunities deserves and demands boldness too.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Achieve institutional advancement by means of deploying AI to accelerate research and provide personalized student tutoring and coaching.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within accelerationist discourse that advocates for leveraging advanced artificial intelligence systems to accelerate academic research and provide personalized student tutoring. Encompasses: Research acceleration, personalized coaching tools.

key_points.point: The document recognizes that AI enables innovative ways for students to learn and experiment, acting as an omnipresent technology that students utilize for curiosity and creative inspiration. The committee desires an educational framework that leans into these technological affordances while adapting courses to be AI-aware. This perspective aligns with viewing AI as a powerful capability enhancer that changes what students need to know and do. Nevertheless, the committee cautions that unrestricted use without intentional pedagogical design can undermine foundational mastery.
key_points.verbatim: While AI is allowing instructors to develop exciting new learning experiences and enabling students to learn and experiment in innovative ways, there have been a number of concerning effects on the life of the campus...
key_points.canonical_proposition: It is necessary that educational institutions embrace AI to enable innovative student experimentation and new learning experiences.
key_points.attribution_text: A Desire within accelerationist discourse that advocates for embracing generative artificial intelligence to create innovative learning experiences and foster student experimentation. Encompasses: Innovative learning experiences, student experimentation.

key_points.point: Instructors can successfully leverage generative AI to develop customized, interactive learning tools and coaching agents that provide tailored guidance and timely support for students exploring complex subject matter. For example, personalized AI coaches in mediator training helped students overcome public speaking anxiety and increased their willingness to practice. Such tools amplify instructional capacity and enable scalable, individualized mentoring across diverse disciplines. However, deploying these systems requires careful design to ensure they complement rather than replace interpersonal engagement. This approach aligns with accelerationist goals of expanding access to high-performance cognitive tools while augmenting human capability.
key_points.verbatim: Many instructors told us that AI helps them develop customized, interactive learning tools that allow students to explore subject content with more depth and for instructors to create learning experiences for their students that are new or newly tailored to each student. With a little guidance, even instructors who are not proficient in software development can customize AI agents to support a subject or research project.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Achieve individualized student mastery by means of deploying customized AI coaching agents and interactive learning tools.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within accelerationist discourse that advocates for deploying customized AI coaching agents and interactive learning tools to accelerate student skill acquisition and provide scalable, individualized mentorship. Encompasses: Personalized feedback loops, AI-driven coaching bots, and scalable interactive modules.

taxonomy_node_candidates.label: Deploy AI as Personalized Workplace Coach and Mentor

key_points.point: Generative AI coding tools enable students to undertake large-scale software projects and build near production-quality artifacts within a single academic term that were previously impossible. This technological capacity transforms capstone courses by allowing learners to focus on high-level system design and real-world implementation rather than getting bogged down in boilerplate syntax. By expanding the scope of student projects, AI acts as a powerful collaborative multiplier that accelerates productivity and creative output. This strategy embodies the accelerationist vision of humans partnering with AI systems to achieve unprecedented technical scale. Nonetheless, educators must ensure foundational conceptual skills keep pace with tool-enabled output.
key_points.verbatim: Today, it’s entirely reasonable to expect students to use AI coding tools to build near production-quality software artifacts in a single academic term. This in turn can make room for deeper experiential learning: students can explore how different designs work in the real world, reflect on cases where certain designs outperform others, and explore how the systems they build work in realistic settings.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Achieve high-complexity project execution by means of integrating AI coding tools into student workflows to build production-quality artifacts.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within accelerationist discourse that advocates for integrating AI coding tools into student workflows to enable the rapid creation of production-quality software artifacts and complex engineering systems. Encompasses: AI-assisted software generation, accelerated project scoping, and high-level system design.

key_points.point: The committee suggests exploring co-op programs, expanded industrial and research opportunities, and experiential learning pathways. This aligns with accelerationist interest in integrating real-world workflows and experiential frameworks into education. However, the report cautions that AI automation could displace student researchers, indicating a friction point between efficiency gains and community preservation. Instructors are nevertheless encouraged to support responsible experimentation in the curriculum.
key_points.verbatim: We also encourage the Institute to explore related efforts to enhance the value of the MIT residential experience, such as establishing co-op programs (which the Institute is actively exploring11), allowing UROP-like experiences to satisfy degree requirements, or expanding industrial/co-op based graduate research programs.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Achieve experiential learning integration by means of expanding co-op programs and industrial research partnerships.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within accelerationist discourse that advocates for expanding industrial and co-op based research programs to enhance practical skill acquisition and bridge academic learning with real-world technological deployment. Encompasses: Co-op programs, experiential learning pathways, and UROP integration.

key_points.point: The committee urges faculty governance to review administrative processes to enable rapid curricular experimentation and the creation of alternative course variants like AI-heavy or AI-light pathways. This reflects an accelerationist push for agile adaptation and fast-paced institutional evolution. Nevertheless, the text notes the tension between moving rapidly and preserving long-term curricular coherence.
key_points.verbatim: We urge faculty governance to review its processes this fall to ensure the presence of efficient pathways for curricular experiments that enable more rapid exploration, paired, of course, with thorough evaluation of the results.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Achieve rapid curricular adaptation by means of streamlining faculty governance processes for experimental course design.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within accelerationist discourse that advocates for streamlining faculty governance processes to enable rapid curricular experimentation and agile adaptation to technological disruption. Encompasses: Curricular experimentation, streamlined governance review, and agile course variant development.

key_points.point: The document highlights that over two-thirds of students believe AI will be critical to their future careers, yet only a fraction feel adequately prepared by the institution. To address this gap, the committee recommends immediately integrating the effective, responsible, and ethical uses of artificial intelligence into student orientation and infusing these competencies throughout the curriculum. By establishing structured educational frameworks for AI fluency, the university can ensure students build a shared sense of competence in assessing and leveraging emerging technologies. This proactive adaptation aligns with accelerationist goals of preparing the workforce for an AI-infused economy rather than retreating from technological integration.
key_points.verbatim: In the fall 2025 Tech Survey, more than two-thirds of students who responded felt that AI would be important in their careers, yet only 25% felt that MIT was adequately preparing them to use AI. The effective, responsible, and ethical uses of AI are distinct – but interrelated. Students need ways to build strength in each area. We recommend immediately integrating these topics into undergraduate and graduate orientation, and infusing them throughout the curriculum as soon as possible, so community members can build a shared sense of competence in assessing and evaluating AI systems.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Educational institutions ought to integrate AI literacy and fluency training across all undergraduate and graduate curricula to prepare students for technology-infused careers.
key_points.attribution_text: A Desire within accelerationist discourse that advocates for the mandatory integration of algorithmic fluency and critical interaction skills into foundational educational curricula. Encompasses: Career preparation, curriculum integration, and student competence building.

key_points.point: The committee recommends funding an AI Implementation Team and AI Fellows composed of staff, postdocs, and students to actively assist instructors in modernizing their courses. Rather than leaving individual educators to struggle with technological transitions alone, this institutional mechanism provides direct support, technical guidance, and implementation expertise based on learning sciences. This strategy operationalizes accelerationist principles by scaling the adoption of advanced AI educational tools and workflows across the entire institution.
key_points.verbatim: We also recommend that MIT fund an AI Implementation Team and AI Fellows – staff members, postdocs, UROPs, and graduate students with the skills to help instructors adapt their courses to AI in ways that make the most of the latest AI technology and are backed by the principles of learning science. Including experts in technology, AI, and learning sciences, the Team and the Fellows would work at three levels: supporting individual instructors; developing campus-wide tools; and serving as implementation experts with an 'ear to the ground' to study how these tools are being used across campus and to what effect.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Institutions should deploy specialized AI implementation teams and fellows to actively assist instructors in modernizing pedagogy with advanced technologies.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within accelerationist discourse that proposes deploying specialized technical teams and faculty fellows to accelerate the integration of AI tools into institutional pedagogy. Encompasses: Implementation teams, faculty support, and pedagogical adaptation.

key_points.point: To overcome the reluctance and hesitation of overworked instructors, the report advocates establishing an AI Pilot Fund to provide financial resources, computing credits, and staffing support. By lowering the economic and logistical barriers to experimentation, this mechanism incentivizes educators to redesign course objectives and explore innovative AI-enabled pedagogies. This economic stimulus approach aligns with accelerationist aims to fast-track technological experimentation and diffusion in higher education.
key_points.verbatim: We recommend that MIT and departments/schools/the college create an AI Pilot Fund that instructors can apply to for resources (such as AI credits, TAs, UROPs, and summer support) to do AI-enabled projects, explore the impact of AI on pedagogy, and create deliberately AI-free experiences.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Universities should establish dedicated pilot funds providing financial and computational resources to incentivize instructors to experiment with AI-enabled pedagogy.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within accelerationist discourse that advocates for establishing targeted pilot funding and computational grants to incentivize rapid pedagogical experimentation with artificial intelligence. Encompasses: Pilot funding, computational credits, and instructor resource grants.

key_points.point: The report stresses the necessity of providing a model-agnostic institutional platform, such as Parley, equipped with free user credits and advanced agentic coding tools. By maintaining first-class access to state-of-the-art models for all community members, the institution mitigates the severe socio-economic inequities that arise when only affluent students can afford commercial subscriptions. This infrastructure-provision strategy ensures broad access to cutting-edge capabilities, supporting the accelerationist goal of universal technological empowerment.
key_points.verbatim: MIT should continue to provide a 'model agnostic' AI platform such as Parley, that does not tie our community to one model provider, and ensure that this platform provides the level of access that our community needs. [...] Because agentic systems and tools are increasingly part of AI practice, whatever systems we employ should provide access to agentic coding and working tools, in addition to chat interfaces.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Institutions must provide universal, model-agnostic access to advanced artificial intelligence platforms and agentic tools to prevent socio-economic performance disparities.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within accelerationist discourse that proposes deploying centralized, model-agnostic AI platforms equipped with agentic coding capabilities to ensure equitable technological access. Encompasses: Model-agnostic platforms, agentic tools, and equitable access.

key_points.point: The MIT committee argues that the Institute must deliberately integrate AI into the classroom, research enterprise, and residential experience to ensure learning and advance discovery. By establishing clear policies and incorporating AI into workflows as a capability enhancer, the academic community can prepare students for an AI-saturated world. This approach balances productivity gains with educational objectives through structured frameworks like standard syllabus policy menus. However, the report cautions that integration requires careful thought regarding boundaries and student skill development.
key_points.verbatim: We must demonstrate how to integrate AI thoughtfully and deliberately into the classroom, the research enterprise, and the experience of residential education in ways that ensure learning, advance discovery, and prepare students for the future.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Integrate AI into educational and research workflows as a capability enhancer by establishing standard syllabus policy menus.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within accelerationist discourse that advocates for the deliberate integration of generative artificial intelligence into educational curricula and research workflows to enhance productivity and prepare students for an AI-driven economy. Encompasses: Standardizing classroom AI policies, leveraging AI for workflow enhancement, and preparing students for professional AI integration.

key_points.point: The committee notes that AI's rapid ascendance is progressing on a timescale too compressed for society to properly observe and analyze its impacts before institutions adapt. To counter disruptive outcomes, the report calls for a humble approach where course corrections are anticipated as the technology evolves. This safety-oriented posture emphasizes understanding systemic impacts on campus life, such as increased isolation and the erosion of student confidence. The committee insists on maintaining human-centric educational values despite the pressures of rapid technological deployment.
key_points.verbatim: In other words, AI is progressing across almost every domain and on a timescale too compressed for society to properly observe and analyze its impacts and then gradually adapt. This suggests our first guiding principle: We offer our proposals in a spirit of humility.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Achieve institutional stability by means of adopting a humble, adaptive regulatory posture toward compressed AI development timelines.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within safetyist discourse that proposes adopting a humble and adaptive institutional posture to manage compressed AI development timelines. Encompasses: Compressed AI timelines, institutional humility, adaptive course corrections.

taxonomy_node_candidates.label: Countering AI-Driven Skill Decay and Cognitive Displacement

Building Adaptive Regulatory Frameworks for AI Development

key_points.point: The report asserts that generative AI has landed abruptly, becoming socially consequential before individuals and institutions have time to adapt. By entering public consciousness rapidly following late 2022, AI has generated immediate rapid changes and long-term tectonic disruptions across educational practices. These unforeseen capabilities disrupt traditional assignments, take-home exams, and study groups, creating an urgent need for institutional reexamination. The committee emphasizes that these shifts challenge decades of community norms regarding rigor and personal integrity.
key_points.verbatim: Other innovations land more abruptly, becoming socially consequential before individuals and institutions have time to adapt. The computer — AI's precursor and key enabler — fits this pattern. Other innovations land more abruptly...
key_points.canonical_proposition: Abrupt technological deployment causes tectonic institutional disruptions before societies can properly analyze and adapt to AI impacts.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within safetyist discourse that asserts abrupt technological deployment causes tectonic institutional disruptions before societies can properly adapt. Encompasses: Abrupt technological deployment, institutional disruption.

Society Cannot Absorb AI Capability Shocks at the Pace They Arrive
Corporate Subsidiary Bankruptcy Arbitrage in Autonomous Deployments

key_points.point: The rapid adoption of generative AI creates a profound risk of cognitive displacement, where students offload essential learning and problem-solving tasks to algorithms, bypassing the productive struggle necessary for intellectual development. This behavioral shift manifests in decreased office hour attendance, reduced online participation, and a breakdown of peer study groups. To counteract skill decay, educational institutions must actively redesign curricula and assessments to ensure that AI augmentation preserves human agency and critical reasoning. Safetyist frameworks demand that technological deployment be paired with structural safeguards that protect human cognitive development. However, institutions must navigate this without falling into nostalgic rejection of technological progress.
key_points.verbatim: Because many students are choosing or feel pressure to shift to learning and problem-solving with AI, in less than three years these technologies have driven major shifts in campus culture, including decreased attendance at office hours, reduced participation in online discussions, and, as we heard anecdotally, a drop in in-person study groups in dorms, libraries, and other study spaces.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Mitigate AI-driven cognitive displacement and skill decay by redesigning academic assessments to protect the cognitive friction necessary for learning.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within safetyist discourse that advocates for monitoring and countering cognitive displacement and skill decay caused by premature AI substitution in human problem-solving workflows. Encompasses: Intelligence displacement spirals, cognitive friction preservation, and curriculum redesign.

taxonomy_node_candidates.label: Countering AI-Driven Skill Decay and Cognitive Displacement
Rapidly Evolving Social Norms to Keep Up with AI
Add Deliberate Speed Bumps to AI-Assisted Decision-Making

key_points.point: Educational institutions ought to preserve and reinvigorate the residential campus experience as a vital social contract centered on shared human presence, mentorship, and community norms. While AI offers efficiency, relying solely on automated transactions threatens to erode the tacit expectations, relationships, and values that inform how students develop ethical judgment and social responsibility. A robust social contract among students, instructors, and the institution is necessary to ensure that technology serves human flourishing rather than replacing interpersonal community. This normative commitment prioritizes holistic human maturation over transactional optimization. The primary caveat is that preserving this model requires proactive institutional intervention against isolating technological habits.
key_points.verbatim: MIT should therefore treat AI not only as a pedagogical or technical challenge, but as a critical opportunity to renew residential education around human presence, shared work, and meaningful mentorship.
key_points.canonical_proposition: It is necessary that educational institutions renew residential education around human presence, shared work, and meaningful mentorship to counter AI-induced isolation.
key_points.attribution_text: A Desire within safetyist discourse that advocates for renewing residential education around human presence, shared work, and meaningful mentorship to counter the isolating effects of AI automation. Encompasses: Institutional social contracts, in-person community building, and human-centered educational norms.

key_points.point: The document asserts that opportunistic or unthinking reliance on generative AI tools diminishes student learning and damages the intellectual community. It argues that genuine learning requires cognitive friction, such as solving proofs or debugging experiments collaboratively. Without this friction, students face skill atrophy and a loss of personal agency.
key_points.verbatim: It’s clear that unthinking, “opportunistic” use of AI tools to complete assignments diminishes what students learn and damages the learning communities they belong to. Learning works when it’s both challenging and social; knowledge is built through cognitive friction, whether that’s disentangling the steps of a mathematical proof with your study group, adjusting an experiment over and over until it works, or having a spirited argument with a peer (rather than getting “the” answer from AI).
key_points.canonical_proposition: Unthinking reliance on AI tools removes cognitive friction, leading directly to diminished student learning and intellectual skill atrophy.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within safetyist discourse that unthinking reliance on generative AI tools eliminates necessary cognitive friction, thereby causing intellectual skill atrophy and eroding the social foundations of learning communities. Encompasses: Cognitive friction, skill atrophy, and AI-mediated learning degradation.

taxonomy_node_candidates.label: AI Dependency Creates a Reinforcing Cycle of Skill Atrophy and Increased Reliance

Intellectual Autonomy in an AI-Saturated World

key_points.point: The committee recommends against relying on automated AI detectors, warning that they trigger an adversarial arms race and result in false positives for non-native English speakers or neurodivergent students. Instead, instructors are advised to foster transparency, clear course policies with explicit rationales, and process-oriented assessments like version histories.
key_points.verbatim: No doubt the tools will improve. Nevertheless, we recommend against relying on AI detectors, as it risks an arms race in which students respond to automated detection by using increasingly powerful “AI humanizers” to remove signals that AI detectors are cued to catch.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Avoid adversarial AI surveillance by means of implementing transparent course policies and process-oriented learning assessments.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within safetyist discourse that advocates against deploying automated AI detectors in favor of transparent course policies, clear rationales, and process-oriented assessments to preserve trust and prevent adversarial policing. Encompasses: Rejection of AI detectors, process evidence tracking, and transparent policy rationales.

key_points.point: The report emphasizes that MIT must act decisively to ensure AI augments human communities rather than quietly replacing them, safeguarding residential education, mentorship, and face-to-face interaction. The ultimate objective is to ensure that technology serves human well-being rather than subordinating human agency.
key_points.verbatim: The challenge for MIT is therefore neither to preserve existing practices unchanged, nor to reject AI tools that may support learning and research. It is to act decisively to ensure that AI augments the human communities through which education happens, rather than quietly replacing them — so that the machines serve us and not the other way round.
key_points.canonical_proposition: AI systems ought to be deliberately designed to augment human residential communities rather than replace interpersonal mentorship and collaboration.
key_points.attribution_text: A Desire within safetyist discourse that prioritizes the active safeguarding of human residential communities, mentorship structures, and interpersonal collaboration against displacement by artificial intelligence systems. Encompasses: Community augmentation, residential education preservation, and human-centric technological subordination.

key_points.point: The report emphasizes the critical distinction between AI augmentation—where technology helps humans perform better work—and automation, which can replace human effort and eliminate the learning that comes from doing the work. Responsible use requires understanding these cognitive boundaries and establishing rigorous academic norms around authorship and disclosure. This focus directly addresses safetyist concerns regarding intelligence displacement and the degradation of human capability through uncritical AI delegation.
key_points.verbatim: Using it responsibly begins with grasping the difference between augmentation and automation when it comes to education: when AI helps a human do better work, versus when it replaces the human (and thereby eliminates the learning that would come from the human doing the work). Responsible use also entails knowing how to disclose AI's contribution honestly across coursework, theses, internal reports, and published research.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Educational policies must enforce a clear distinction between human augmentation and cognitive automation to prevent the erosion of foundational learning.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within safetyist discourse that advocates for establishing institutional policies distinguishing beneficial cognitive augmentation from detrimental automation to preserve human skill development. Encompasses: Augmentation versus automation, cognitive preservation, and disclosure norms.

key_points.point: The committee recommends establishing an ongoing AI and education committee tasked with monitoring off-campus and on-campus impacts, evaluating technological changes, and updating institutional policies based on evolving evidence. This institutional governance body acts as a centralized oversight mechanism to continuously assess safety risks, pedagogical disruptions, and ethical concerns. Such ongoing monitoring structure reflects safetyist demands for adaptive, rigorous oversight as AI capabilities rapidly evolve.
key_points.verbatim: To put our recommendations into practice, MIT should establish an ongoing committee. It will serve to monitor the on- and off-campus impacts of AI; evaluate changes in AI models and technology; and incorporate evolving evidence from the economy, learning sciences, and campus experience into policies and practices.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Universities should establish permanent governance committees to continuously monitor technological advancements and coordinate institutional safety policies.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within safetyist discourse that proposes creating dedicated institutional oversight bodies to monitor artificial intelligence impacts and continuously update governance policies. Encompasses: Ongoing committee oversight, impact monitoring, and policy coordination.

key_points.point: The document mandates that all student theses include a formal statement detailing how artificial intelligence was used in their production, explicitly prohibiting listing AI as a co-author. This policy establishes clear boundaries around intellectual property and academic integrity, ensuring transparency in research dissemination. Implementing mandatory disclosure requirements aligns with safetyist objectives to maintain rigorous human accountability and provenance tracking in scientific output.
key_points.verbatim: All theses should include a statement about how AI was used in the production of the thesis. AI should never be listed as a co-author. Most journals and conferences also require acknowledgment of AI use, and some prohibit certain use cases, so researchers should check guidelines before preparing manuscripts for publication.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Academic institutions must mandate transparent disclosure statements regarding AI utilization in all research publications and student theses.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within safetyist discourse that advocates for mandatory disclosure policies regarding AI usage in academic research and thesis production to maintain integrity and provenance. Encompasses: Thesis disclosure statements, authorship boundaries, and research integrity.

key_points.point: The report highlights the severe privacy risks associated with commercial AI tools, noting that default platform configurations often capture user chat sessions and sensitive data for training purposes. To protect personal confidentiality and institutional intellectual property, the institute must enforce strict data protection policies and prioritize model-agnostic platforms that prevent unauthorized data harvesting. This technical safeguarding approach addresses core safetyist concerns regarding data surveillance and privacy erosion.
key_points.verbatim: One concern about commercial AI tools is that sensitive data may be incorporated into their training sets. Most plans, especially paid ones, allow users to deliberately disable the capture of their data for training purposes – but the default is often to record user sessions for training. This leads to the possibility of private, sensitive data from MIT users finding its way into the answers that these models provide.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Institutions must enforce strict privacy controls and default-private settings to prevent commercial AI platforms from harvesting sensitive user data for model training.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within safetyist discourse that proposes enforcing stringent data privacy standards and model-agnostic configurations to prevent unauthorized harvesting of sensitive user information for training datasets. Encompasses: Data privacy protection, training set exclusion, and confidentiality safeguards.

key_points.point: The report highlights widespread community concern regarding the impact of AI on cognitive development, critical thinking, and long-term skill acquisition. To counter potential skill decay, instructors are urged to rethink assessments and establish clear boundaries on AI use, such as restricted support tool policies that prohibit submitting full AI-generated solutions as one's own. These measures aim to preserve the cognitive struggle necessary for deep learning while monitoring the technical and durable human skills demanded by industry. Nonetheless, policing out-of-class use remains exceptionally difficult, creating risks of undetected violations.
key_points.verbatim: Respondents expressed concern that reliance on AI could reduce critical thinking, writing ability, creativity, reasoning, and long-term skill development, or otherwise diminish the educational value of coursework.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Counter AI-driven cognitive displacement and skill decay by redesigning academic assessments and establishing strict usage boundaries.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within safetyist discourse that addresses cognitive displacement and skill decay by redesigning academic assessments and enforcing strict usage boundaries to preserve critical thinking. Encompasses: Mitigating overreliance on AI tools, protecting cognitive development, and restructuring academic integrity policies.

Countering AI-Driven Skill Decay and Cognitive Displacement
Build Structured Peer Review to Prevent AI Safety Groupthink

key_points.point: The report documents that overreliance on chatbots can trigger cognitive surrender, where students fall back on AI at the first hint of struggle. The committee notes that many uses of AI deprive students of the opportunity to learn, diminishing critical thinking, weakening memory, eroding confidence, and undermining mastery. Furthermore, the reliance on automated systems displaces peer-to-peer connections such as study groups and decreases interactions between students and instructors. This reliance threatens to deskill learners and isolate them within the educational environment.
key_points.verbatim: Getting the right answer from a chatbot can create the illusion of learning — but it can also trigger 'cognitive surrender', where students fall back on AI at the first hint of struggle.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Overreliance on AI chatbots triggers cognitive surrender and diminishes critical thinking by removing necessary productive struggle.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within skeptic discourse that asserts overreliance on artificial intelligence chatbots triggers cognitive surrender and diminishes critical thinking by removing productive struggle. Encompasses: Cognitive surrender, illusion of learning, erosion of critical thinking.

key_points.point: The committee observes that AI is upending foundational elements of the MIT educational experience, making it much harder to assess student progress reliably. Traditional assessments like problem sets and take-home exams are compromised when unrestricted AI use allows students to bypass core intellectual work. This dynamic fosters an underground river of mutual suspicion, where instructors police cheating and students fear wrongful accusation, eroding the social contract between teachers and learners. The illusion of learning created by chatbots thus directly undermines genuine academic inquiry.
key_points.verbatim: While AI is allowing instructors to develop exciting new learning experiences and enabling students to learn and experiment in innovative ways, there have been a number of concerning effects on the life of the campus, including signs that AI is: Upending foundational elements of the MIT educational experience...
key_points.canonical_proposition: Unrestricted AI use undermines traditional assessment reliability and erodes the social contract between instructors and students.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within skeptic discourse that maintains unrestricted artificial intelligence use undermines traditional assessment reliability and erodes educational social contracts. Encompasses: Assessment reliability failure, erosion of academic social contracts.

taxonomy_node_candidates.label: AI Automation Breaks the Work-to-Prosperity Social Bargain

key_points.point: Generative AI systems provide immediate, frictionless solutions to complex homework, proof, and coding assignments, thereby removing the cognitive friction and productive struggle required for deep learning. When students bypass this mental effort to maximize efficiency, they undermine their long-term mastery and intellectual autonomy. This transactional mindset reduces education to an optimizable commodity and impairs the development of rigorous critical thinking. Skeptical analysis highlights that offloading analytical tasks to AI actively degrades baseline human capabilities. Nonetheless, students face intense scheduling pressures that incentivize this form of cognitive offloading.
key_points.verbatim: A fundamental danger, as we’ve discussed, is that AI can allow students to bypass learning. Equally concerning is that students may internalize a transactional model in which assignments are outputs, teachers are evaluators, peers are optional, and knowledge (or an MIT degree) is an optimizable commodity to be acquired or produced as efficiently as possible.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Providing frictionless AI solutions allows students to bypass cognitive struggle, which severely impedes deep learning and long-term knowledge retention.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within skeptic discourse that providing frictionless AI solutions allows students to bypass necessary cognitive struggle, severely impeding deep learning and knowledge retention. Encompasses: Cognitive offloading, transactional educational models, and the erosion of intellectual rigor.

key_points.point: Instructors must abandon vulnerable, out-of-class assessment methods like traditional problem sets and take-home exams in favor of AI-resilient evaluation formats such as oral exams, semester portfolios, and supervised in-class work. Because LLMs can competently complete standard undergraduate assignments, traditional grading mechanisms have lost their validity for measuring genuine student understanding. While shifting toward in-class evaluations or oral defenses introduces tactical challenges and reduces time for deep reflection, it remains essential for preserving assessment integrity. Institutions must resource these more intensive evaluation methods to ensure degrees reflect true competence. The risk is that overemphasizing rapid, high-stakes testing may incentivize superficial cramming over sustained inquiry.
key_points.verbatim: We urge instructors to consider forms of assessment that are less vulnerable to AI, and more valuable for learning, such as oral exams, semester portfolios, and out-of-class assignments paired with in-class conversations. This likely means that resources such as TAs and class time will become more central to evaluation and also raises the question of whether we should find ways to limit class sizes.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Protect assessment integrity by replacing AI-vulnerable take-home work with AI-resilient evaluation formats such as oral exams and supervised portfolios.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within skeptic discourse that advocates for replacing AI-vulnerable take-home work with AI-resilient evaluation formats such as oral exams, supervised portfolios, and in-class conversations to ensure genuine assessment integrity. Encompasses: Assessment redesign, oral examinations, and faculty-led verification of student competence.

key_points.point: Generative AI systems provide answer-first outputs that bypass the necessary mental struggle of inquiry, which undermines deep learning and critical reasoning. When students rely on AI to instantly generate solutions, they miss out on learning how research questions are formed and how judgment develops.
key_points.verbatim: The danger is not only that students would have fewer opportunities to conduct research, but fewer opportunities to become participants in research communities. ... Students learn not only methods and technical competencies, but also how research questions are formed, how judgment develops, how mistakes are constructively interpreted, how credit is shared, how disagreement is handled, and how knowledge is collectively produced.
key_points.canonical_proposition: AI-driven answer generation bypasses intellectual struggle, thereby undermining the development of deep research judgment and inquiry skills.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within skeptic discourse that automated answer generation bypasses essential intellectual struggle, undermining the cognitive and social processes through which research judgment and deep inquiry skills are formed. Encompasses: Answer-first architectures, suppression of inquiry, and erosion of research judgment.

key_points.point: The committee recommends maintaining rigorous in-person proctored exams, collaborative hands-on lab spaces, and oral evaluations rather than relying on flawed lockdown browsers or remote surveillance tools. These measures protect assessment integrity while fostering genuine human connection.
key_points.verbatim: The committee recommends that MIT study such tools, but notes that the current generation is buggy, error-prone and feels like surveillance. At least for now, in-person proctored exams – the current norm at MIT – are a better choice in most cases, though they will require appropriate in-person spaces.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Achieve assessment integrity by means of prioritizing in-person proctored evaluations and hands-on collaborative spaces over remote surveillance tools.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within skeptic discourse that advocates for prioritizing in-person proctored evaluations and collaborative physical spaces over remote surveillance technologies to maintain assessment integrity and trust. Encompasses: In-person proctored exams, collaborative physical spaces, and rejection of digital surveillance tools.

key_points.point: The report asserts that instructors should clearly explain the pedagogical rationales behind AI restrictions so that students understand why doing the work themselves is in their own self-interest. This fosters self-awareness and intellectual autonomy rather than compliance with arbitrary rules.
key_points.verbatim: For example, if an instructor wants to ban the use of generative AI tools instead of simply declaring that AI use is a form of cheating, it’s more effective to explain how generative AI tools shortcut students' ability to learn the fundamentals of the course or to practice solving the kind of problems they will encounter in exams, future classes, and the real world.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Instructors ought to articulate transparent pedagogical rationales for AI restrictions to cultivate student intellectual autonomy and self-awareness.
key_points.attribution_text: A Desire within skeptic discourse that instructors articulate transparent pedagogical rationales for AI restrictions to cultivate student intellectual autonomy, self-awareness, and intrinsic motivation rather than blind compliance. Encompasses: Pedagogical rationale articulation, intellectual autonomy, and intrinsic learning motivation.

key_points.point: Students and instructors express deep skepticism regarding the overuse of artificial intelligence in educational settings, noting that it can make teaching feel impersonal and devalued. When educators rely on automated systems to generate lectures, slides, and feedback while imposing strict restrictions on students, it creates a perceived double standard that alienates the academic community. This empirical observation captures the skeptic concern that excessive reliance on AI diminishes authentic human engagement and erodes relational trust in education.
key_points.verbatim: While AI can be a remarkably useful tool to help instructors improve lecture notes, generate slides, and create animations or simulations, students made clear that its over-use in the classroom can make them feel that teaching is not a priority for their instructors. A common refrain: 'Why should I bother coming to class or doing the work if the teacher is just going to give an AI-generated lecture?'
key_points.canonical_proposition: Over-reliance on artificial intelligence in instructional delivery diminishes student engagement and degrades the perceived quality of human-led education.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within skeptic discourse that observes how the integration of automated instructional tools diminishes interpersonal connection and devalues the educational experience. Encompasses: Classroom alienation, instructional over-reliance, and perceived teaching degradation.

key_points.point: The committee documents widespread community objection to the foundational training practices of commercial AI corporations, which harvest vast quantities of internet data without consent, attribution, or compensation to original creators. Consequently, many community members refuse to utilize AI systems on ethical grounds. This finding highlights the skeptic argument that the expansion of AI models relies on extractive and inequitable data practices that infringe upon intellectual property and creator rights.
key_points.verbatim: As we learned from both listening sessions and survey results, many people at MIT object to the way most AI models were trained – by reading vast amounts of data from the internet, often without the authors' explicit consent. Some community members decline to use AI at all because they object to how the data has been harvested without benefit or attribution to its creators.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Commercial AI model training practices rely on the unauthorized harvesting of internet data without proper attribution or compensation to creators.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within skeptic discourse that highlights the exploitative nature of large-scale web scraping and data harvesting for AI training without creator consent or remuneration. Encompasses: Unauthorized data harvesting, lack of attribution, and creator exploitation.

key_points.point: The document notes that community members harbor serious apprehensions regarding the immense environmental footprint of AI infrastructure, including the severe energy and water consumption of data centers and the hardware resource demands of continuous model training. These tangible ecological costs illustrate the skeptic position that the rapid scaling of artificial intelligence imposes profound negative externalities on local communities and global sustainability.
key_points.verbatim: Many community members shared serious concerns about the environmental costs of AI and the impact of data centers on communities where they're built. Issues include data centers' energy and water consumption, the impact of their construction, and the materials used to build their hardware.
key_points.canonical_proposition: The training and operation of artificial intelligence infrastructure impose severe environmental costs through intensive energy and water consumption.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within skeptic discourse that documents the substantial environmental externalities and resource depletion caused by artificial intelligence data centers and model training. Encompasses: Environmental impact, energy consumption, and infrastructure externalities.

key_points.point: The report highlights the complex ethical dilemma surrounding institutional logging and auditing of AI chat systems, where users often share deeply personal, psychological, and sensitive queries. While administrators might wish to monitor system usage to ensure learning goals are met, doing so directly conflicts with the absolute necessity of preserving user confidentiality and psychological safety. This tension reflects skeptic concerns regarding institutional surveillance and the erosion of personal privacy in AI-saturated environments.
key_points.verbatim: Because Parley is an MIT-administered system, one opportunity it provides is to audit usage of AI models; in theory, IS&T can see every request from users to Parley and responses from the backend API models. MIT therefore needs to establish a clear policy about what types of logging and auditing will be allowed. There are competing interests: On one hand, users may want to use these models to ask private or personally sensitive questions with the expectation that their data will be confidential. On the other, instructors may find it valuable to see how their students are using AI chat sessions or logs to see if learning goals are being met.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Institutions must carefully balance instructional auditing against the protection of personal confidentiality when administering centralized AI chat platforms.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within skeptic discourse that advocates for establishing rigorous governance boundaries around platform logging and auditing to protect personal confidentiality from institutional surveillance. Encompasses: Platform auditing, user confidentiality, and surveillance resistance.

key_points.point: Survey data from the MIT community reveal that approximately 90% of undergraduates are concerned about overreliance on large language models, with many fearing it degrades critical thinking and long-term skill development. Furthermore, respondents note that AI tools are frequently unpredictable and unreliable, with significantly more individuals rating them as unreliable rather than trustworthy. These immediate, measurable friction points demonstrate that unrestricted AI delegation poses direct risks to human analytical capabilities and academic rigor. However, students also recognize that AI proficiency is increasingly vital for their future careers despite these cognitive hazards.
key_points.verbatim: Significantly more respondents felt that AI was unpredictable and unreliable than felt it was trustworthy and reliable, with 39% selecting a 1 or 2 vs 21% selecting a 4 or 5 on this axis.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Overreliance on unreliable AI systems degrades human critical thinking, analytical capabilities, and long-term skill development.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within skeptic discourse that asserts system reliance on unreliable artificial intelligence models actively degrades baseline human critical thinking and decision-making capabilities. Encompasses: Systemic overreliance on language models, unreliability of generated outputs, and degradation of analytical skills.

factual_claims.claim: Generative artificial intelligence experienced its widespread public birth with the release of ChatGPT in late 2022, accumulating over a billion users in less than four years. This rapid consumer adoption far outpaces traditional technological diffusion rates, leaving institutions with compressed timelines for adaptation.

MIT students use generative AI frequently and pervasively, exhibiting strongly mixed feelings ranging from curiosity and creative inspiration to resignation, concern, and anxiety regarding its impact on their education.
factual_claims.claim_label: Pervasive Student AI Usage and Mixed Sentiments

factual_claims.claim: Generative artificial intelligence technologies, including large language models, are currently capable of producing credible solutions and reasonable responses to almost any written assignment in an undergraduate curriculum, including essays, mathematics and science problems, logical proofs, and coding tasks.

category_criteria.observational_grounding: Direct observation from faculty and committee evaluation across MIT undergraduate curricula.
category_criteria.measurement_validity: Confirmed by the successful automated completion of standard departmental p-sets and coding exams.
category_criteria.generalizability: Applies broadly across STEM and humanities undergraduate coursework.

factual_claims.claim: Within a period of less than three years following the widespread availability of generative AI, undergraduate adoption has driven major negative shifts in campus culture, specifically including decreased attendance at faculty office hours, reduced participation in online discussions, and a noticeable drop in in-person study groups.
factual_claims.claim_label: AI Adoption Drives Campus Social Disengagement

category_criteria.observational_grounding: Anecdotal and observational reports gathered by the committee from instructors and students across campus.
category_criteria.measurement_validity: Tracked via proxies such as office hour attendance logs and study space utilization.
category_criteria.generalizability: Reflects systemic behavioral changes across the undergraduate student body.

factual_claims.claim: MIT's Undergraduate Research Opportunities Program (UROP) directly engages 93 percent of undergraduates and 58 percent of faculty in frontline, faculty-led research.

category_criteria.observational_grounding: Institutional administrative metrics tracking UROP enrollment and faculty participation.
category_criteria.measurement_validity: Direct percentage calculation of undergraduate and faculty headcounts.
category_criteria.generalizability: Specific to the MIT institutional environment.

factual_claims.claim: Undergraduate research opportunities like UROP provide students with essential entry into intellectual communities, teaching them research methodologies, judgment development, constructive interpretation of mistakes, and collaborative knowledge production.

category_criteria.falsifiability: verifiable through tracking student outcomes and community integration
category_criteria.generality: applicable across higher education research environments

factual_claims.claim: AI detection tools are prone to false positives that misidentify the writing of non-native English speakers or neurodivergent students as machine-generated text, and they easily prompt an adversarial detection arms race.
factual_claims.claim_label: Limitations and Risks of AI Detectors

category_criteria.observational_basis: empirical evaluation of commercial AI detection software limitations
category_criteria.falsifiability: testable via false positive rate measurements across demographic groups
category_criteria.generality: broadly applicable to academic integrity enforcement in digital environments

factual_claims.claim: In the fall 2025 Tech Survey, more than two-thirds of responding students indicated that artificial intelligence would be important in their professional careers, yet only 25% felt that MIT was adequately preparing them to utilize it.
factual_claims.claim_label: Student Survey on Career Importance Versus Preparedness

category_criteria.observational_basis: Institutional student survey data collected in Fall 2025.
category_criteria.quantifiable_metric: Two-thirds career importance versus 25 percent institutional preparation.
category_criteria.falsifiability: Verifiable through institutional survey archives and response datasets.

factual_claims.claim: Commercial generative AI subscription plans from leading providers such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic cost up to $200 per month for top-tier individual access as of June 2026, with heavy API users spending thousands more.
factual_claims.claim_label: Commercial AI Subscription and API Costs

category_criteria.observational_basis: Market pricing of commercial AI provider offerings as of mid-2026.
category_criteria.quantifiable_metric: Subscription pricing up to $200 monthly per user.
category_criteria.falsifiability: Verifiable through commercial vendor pricing schedules.

factual_claims.claim: MIT's Information Systems and Technology (IS&T) provides the Parley system, which grants campus users access to multiple commercial and open-source models with up to $30 per month in free credits, complemented by API access introduced in Summer 2026.
factual_claims.claim_label: MIT Parley System Access and Credit Allocation

category_criteria.observational_basis: Institutional IT deployment specifications and resource allocations.
category_criteria.quantifiable_metric: Thirty dollars monthly credit allowance per user.
category_criteria.falsifiability: Verifiable through institutional IS&T service documentation.

factual_claims.claim: In the Spring 2026 MIT survey, 44% of respondents reported using ChatGPT 'Often' or 'Very Often', with undergraduate usage reaching high levels across daily and weekly frequencies.
factual_claims.claim_label: High Frequency ChatGPT Usage Among MIT Students

category_criteria.observational_basis: Campus-wide survey of 1632 respondents representing students and instructors.

factual_claims.claim: Approximately 10% of survey respondents who wrote in concerns about AI cited the potential negative impact of reliance on AI on student learning, critical thinking, writing ability, and cognitive development.
factual_claims.claim_label: Community Concern Over AI Impact on Cognitive Development

category_criteria.observational_basis: Open-ended write-in responses from the Spring 2026 AI Usage and Attitudes Survey.

unmapped_concepts.suggested_description: A situation concept that explores the systemic breakdown and necessary renegotiation of trust, norms, and behavioral expectations between educators and students in response to pervasive artificial intelligence. Encompasses: Academic integrity norms, mutual suspicion dynamics, collaborative educational pacts. Excludes: Technical alignment verification, automated grading protocols.
unmapped_concepts.concept: The document highlights how unauthorized AI use and policing mechanisms create an underground river of mutual suspicion that erodes the traditional social contract between instructors and students, necessitating an explicit renegotiation of classroom norms.
unmapped_concepts.reason: Captures the sociological and relational disruption on campuses caused by AI adoption, distinct from purely cognitive or technical alignment models.
unmapped_concepts.Accelerationist Interpretation: Accelerationists view the erosion of the old social contract as a healthy and inevitable destruction of outdated industrial-era pedagogical constraints, clearing the path for dynamic, highly customized, and AI-integrated mentor-student relationships.
unmapped_concepts.Safetyist Interpretation: Safetyists interpret the breakdown of classroom trust as a dangerous indicator of institutional destabilization, warning that mutual suspicion and student isolation threaten the core ethical foundation of higher education.
unmapped_concepts.Skeptic Interpretation: Skeptics view the fractured social contract as confirmation that generative AI inherently damages human relationships and academic integrity, substituting authentic pedagogical mentorship with transactional interactions mediated by unreliable algorithms.
